title: Remaining useful life: what an ML model actually hands you

blocks.text: 7.3.2 Remaining Useful Life: What an ML Model Actually Hands You

GridCap's data science team has trained a model on sensor readings and maintenance records, and it now predicts a **remaining useful life** (RUL) for every asset: "A004: 1 year. A006: 1 year. A008: 25 years." A director reads the list and asks for A004 and A006 to be replaced this year, since they "have one year left." Lesson 1.1.2 already noticed that A004's RUL of 1 sits next to a PoF of only 3.4%. This lesson explains why that is not a contradiction, what an RUL number is, what you must ask before using one, and how to turn it into a curve that the risk coefficients of lesson 7.3.4 can use, in four rules.

GridCap is a fictional utility generated for this course; its assets and predictions describe no real company. The asset IDs here are the tiny portfolio's (A004 a breaker, A006 a transformer); the small and medium portfolios reuse the same IDs for other assets, and the section that counts the small portfolio names none of them.
RUL Is One Number Taken From a Remaining-Life Distribution

An asset of age $`a`$ that is working today has a **remaining life** $`T - a`$: the years until it fails. Like the lifetime $`T`$ of lesson 7.3.1, it is random. Its distribution follows from the failure curve by the same conditioning that gave next year's PoF: the chance that the asset is still working $`r`$ years from now, given that it works today, is
P(T > a + r \mid T > a) = \frac{R(a + r)}{R(a)}
An RUL is one number chosen to summarize that distribution. There are several natural choices, and they are different numbers:

items: the **median remaining life** $`m`$, the $`r`$ at which that ratio falls to one half. For the Weibull, $`R(a+m)/R(a) = 1/2`$ means $`((a+m)/\eta)^\beta - (a/\eta)^\beta = \ln 2`$, so
the **mean remaining life** (or **mean residual life**), the average of $`T - a`$ over the assets still working at age $`a`$: $`\int_a^\infty R(u)\,du \,/\, R(a)`$;
a **quantile** such as P10, the $`r`$ by which the chance of having failed reaches 10%, a cautious planning figure; or P90, by which it reaches 90%.

blocks.text: scipy computes the others. `isf` is the **inverse survival function**: `curve.isf(p)` is the age at which the survival function equals `p`. To find where the conditional ratio falls to $`1 - q`$, ask for the age where $`R`$ equals $`(1 - q) R(a)`$. The mean uses `expect`, which averages a function over the curve; with `lb=a` and `conditional=True` it averages only over lifetimes beyond $`a`$:
mean = curve.expect(lambda t: t, lb=a.age, conditional=True) - a.age
Here is every tiny asset's remaining-life distribution next to the RUL the GridCap data carries:

Three things to see. First, the spread is wide: A008's remaining life runs from 5 years (P10) to 67 years (P90). One number cannot carry that. Second, mean and median differ, by up to 5.7 years here (A008), so "RUL 20" means different things to two teams that use different statistics. Third, A004's curve gives a median remaining life of 17.6 years, and its RUL says 1. Both cannot describe the same belief about the asset; the next rule explains where the 1 came from.

Ask What the Number Is: Which Statistic, Which End Point, What Error

An RUL from a machine-learning model is the output of a regression trained on past assets, and each design choice in that training changes what the number means. Before an RUL enters a plan, get written answers to four questions.

items: **Which statistic?** Mean, median, a quantile, or "the model's output" with no stated meaning. A regression trained to minimize squared error estimates something like a conditional mean; one trained on a quantile loss estimates that quantile.

**Until what?** "Useful" life often ends at a threshold, such as a health index below a limit, a dissolved-gas reading above one or a condition grade of 5, not at a failure. An asset at its threshold is due for attention, not certain to fail.

**Trained on what?** Assets still in service are censored, exactly as in lesson 7.3.1's fit. A model trained only on assets that already failed learns that assets fail young. Many models also cap their target or their output at a ceiling or a floor.

**How wrong is it?** An interval (say P10 to P90) per asset, or at least the error on held-out assets by age band. Prognostics always carries uncertainty, and a point estimate without its error invites the director's reading of "1 year left."

blocks.text: GridCap's RUL answers the third question badly, and it is worth seeing how, because real predictions fail the same way. The course's generator, which plays the role of the ML model, sets
\text{RUL} = \max\big(1,\ \lfloor \eta - a + \varepsilon \rfloor\big), \qquad \varepsilon \text{ uniform on } [-4, 4]

with $`\lfloor\cdot\rfloor`$ cutting toward zero (Python's `int`). So the GridCap RUL is "years until the asset reaches its characteristic life," with noise, cut to whole years and floored at 1. For an asset younger than $`\eta`$ that lands near the curve's median remaining life. For one already past $`\eta`$, $`\eta - a`$ is negative and the floor turns it into 1, whatever the curve says. Across the small portfolio:

38 assets; 10 have RUL 1, the floor the prediction cannot go below
  their curves' median remaining life: 3.2 to 21.5 years
the other 28: RUL minus the curve's median, on average +0.4 years

Away from the floor, the RUL tracks the curve's median well (within 0.4 years on average). At the floor it carries no information: ten assets read "1 year," and their own curves give them median remaining lives from 3.2 to 21.5 years. A director who funds "everything with RUL 1" funds a list the prediction cannot rank. That is the answer to the scenario: A004 is old for its kind, it is past the age the RUL measures to, and its RUL hit the floor. Its PoF of 3.4% comes from the curve, which says a breaker of 62 that is still working is likely to keep working for many years.
RUL Alone Does Not Fix the PoF: the Shape Decides

Planning needs a probability for each year (lesson 7.3.1), and the tempting shortcut is a mapping "RUL to PoF": a short RUL means a high PoF. But a median remaining life is one point of the remaining-life distribution, and many curves pass through the same point. Take two assets of the same age, 30, both with a median remaining life of exactly 10 years, one with shape 1 and one with shape 6. For each, the program finds the scale that gives that median with scipy's root finder `brentq`, which searches an interval for the value where a function crosses zero:
eta = brentq(lambda e: residual_median(AGE, beta, e) - RUL, 1, 500)

both assets: age 30, median remaining life 10 years
  beta 1.0: eta  14.4, PoF next year 0.067, fails within 5 years 0.293
  beta 6.0: eta  41.2, PoF next year 0.032, fails within 5 years 0.204

Same age, same RUL, and next year's PoF differs by a factor of two. With shape 1 failures come at a steady rate, so some come early; with shape 6 they bunch near the median, so the next year is fairly safe and the risk is concentrated 8 to 12 years out. An RUL becomes a PoF only together with a shape. Some interview notes say PoF "increases exponentially as RUL approaches 0"; no such rule exists without a curve, and with a Weibull curve the hazard grows as a power of age (lesson 7.3.1).
To Use an RUL, Make It a Point on a Curve

When the analytics team supplies both a predicted RUL for each asset and a fleet shape $`\beta`$ for its kind, the two can be combined: choose the scale $`\eta`$ that makes the RUL the median remaining life of an asset of this age. From $`((a+m)/\eta)^\beta - (a/\eta)^\beta = \ln 2`$ with $`m = \text{RUL}`$:
\eta = \left( \frac{(a + \text{RUL})^{\beta} - a^{\beta}}{\ln 2} \right)^{1/\beta}

The asset now has its own curve, consistent with its prediction, and every number lesson 7.3.1 reads from a curve (next year's PoF, the hazard, the chance of failing within five years) follows. The program checks with scipy that the RUL really is the median of the new curve, then compares the scale and the PoF with the ones GridCap's curve gives directly:

eta = eta_from_rul(a.age, a.rul, a.weibull_beta)
    curve = weibull_min(c=a.weibull_beta, scale=eta)
    assert abs(curve.sf(a.age + a.rul) / curve.sf(a.age) - 0.5) < 1e-9     # RUL is the median

For five assets the two sources roughly agree. For A004 and A006 the RUL of 1 becomes a PoF of exactly 0.5 next year: a median remaining life of one year *is* a 50% chance of failing within the year. That shows what the floored prediction claims if you take it at its word, and why you must not: the curve built from the assets' history says 3.4% and 9.5%. When an RUL and a curve disagree this much, the answer is a question to the analytics team, not a choice made quietly in the optimization code. Lesson 7.3.4 solves the plan with both versions and shows how much it moves.

Summary

items: **RUL is one number taken from a remaining-life distribution.** The median, the mean and P10 or P90 of $`R(a+r)/R(a)`$ are different numbers, and the spread can be decades.

**Ask what the number is: which statistic, which end point, what error.** And how the training treated assets still in service. GridCap's RUL is $`\eta - a`$ plus noise, floored at 1, so its floor hides a 3- to 21-year range of medians.
**RUL alone does not fix the PoF: the shape decides.** Same age and same median, PoF 6.7% or 3.2%.

**To use an RUL, make it a point on a curve.** With a fleet shape, $`\eta = (((a+\text{RUL})^\beta - a^\beta)/\ln 2)^{1/\beta}`$ makes the RUL the median, and every probability follows from that curve.

rows: still working $`r`$ years on, given working at $`a`$
remaining life by which the chance of failure is $`q`$

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [Wikipedia, Survival analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Survival_analysis) (the distribution of the future lifetime given survival to $`t_0`$, and the mean residual lifetime $`\int_{t_0}^\infty S(u)\,du / S(t_0)`$); [Wikipedia, Remaining useful life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remaining_useful_life) (RUL as a predicted time, data-driven, physics-based and hybrid estimation, and why prognostics always carries uncertainty); [SciPy, `scipy.stats.weibull_min`](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.weibull_min.html) (`sf`, `isf`, `expect` and the other methods used here); [NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, the Weibull distribution](https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/apr/section1/apr162.htm) (the reliability function and median the conditioning starts from).
Challenges

items: A model reports RUL as P10, not the median. Rewrite `eta_from_rul` for it. Which assets' scales grow and which shrink compared with the median version?
An asset of age 40 has a predicted median RUL of 20 years, and the team gives no shape. Compute next year's PoF for shapes 1.5, 2.5 and 3.5. What would you report to the director?
Write the four questions of this lesson as a one-page data contract the analytics team signs before their RUL enters the plan.

blocks.text: Design Note: Keep the Prediction and the Plan Apart

It is tempting to fit the RUL-to-PoF mapping inside the optimization code, a sigmoid here, a lookup table there, so that the model "uses the ML output directly." This course keeps them apart: the analytics side delivers curves (or RUL plus shape plus its definition), a separate, tested step turns them into coefficients, and the model only reads coefficients. When a plan looks wrong, lesson 1.1.2's question, whether the coefficient, the rule or the objective is at fault, then has an answer you can check: the coefficient step has its own tests against scipy, like the ones in this lesson's practices.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change.

**rul_distribution.py.** Prints each tiny asset's RUL beside the median, mean, P10 and P90 of its remaining life (*RUL Is One Number*). *Try:* Add a P50 column with `residual_quantile` and predict whether it equals the median column.

**rul_vs_curve.py.** Counts the small portfolio's assets at the RUL floor and compares the rest with their curves' medians (*Ask What the Number Is*). *Try:* Repeat it on the medium portfolio. Predict whether the share at the floor goes up or down.

**same_rul_different_pof.py.** Builds two curves with the same age and median remaining life and different shapes (*RUL Alone Does Not Fix the PoF*). *Try:* Add the shape 2.5. Predict where its PoF falls between the two.

**rul_to_curve.py.** Solves each tiny asset's scale from its RUL and compares the PoF with the given curve's (*To Use an RUL, Make It a Point on a Curve*). *Try:* Replace every RUL of 1 by the curve's median before solving. Predict A004's new PoF.
**asset_curves.py.** The module's library, with `residual_median` and `eta_from_rul`.
